summary: The Bahmani Sultanate was born on 3 August 1347, when rebel officers of the Delhi Sultanate in the Deccan crowned Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu) as Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah, with his capital at Gulbarga. The first independent Muslim sultanate of the Deccan, it fought Vijayanagara and Warangal for over a century, moved its capital to Bidar around 1429 and reached its greatest extent under the minister Mahmud Gawan. Factional strife and Gawan's execution in 1481 broke it apart: its governors declared independence from 1490, and it dissolved into the five Deccan Sultanates by 1527.
details: Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah died in 1358 and was succeeded by his son Mohammed Shah I, who spent much of his reign suppressing banditry and fighting his Hindu neighbours, Vijayanagara and, at times, Warangal. Warangal was then ruled by Kapaya Nayaka, a Telugu king of the post-Kakatiya era. He reportedly gave the sultan a jewelled throne, the Takht-e-Firoza or Turquoise Throne. According to the historian Firishta, it replaced Bahman Shah's silver throne on 23 March 1363. The gift marked Bahmani superiority over Warangal, the eastern rival the sultanate would finally conquer some sixty years later.

Gulbarga, which the founder called Hasanabad, was the Bahmani capital, where all his coins were minted. In 1367 Mohammed Shah I built its Jama Masjid with the help of a Persian architect, Rafi of Qazvin. The mosque reflected the Persianate culture of the Bahmani court, where Persian was the official language and the Persian new year, Nowruz, was celebrated; Mohammed Shah had even ascended the throne on Nowruz. Soldiers, scholars and saints moved from Delhi and northern India to the new Deccan capital, which became the heart of a distinctive Indo-Persian culture in the south.

Mohammed Shah I fought savage wars with Vijayanagara over the Tungabhadra-Krishna doab, the Godavari basin and the Marathwada country. The historian Firishta wrote that the population of the Carnatic took generations to recover. At the Battle of Adoni in 1368 the Bahmani army used a train of artillery against Vijayanagara. This is often called the first recorded use of firearms in South Asia, though the historian Iqtidar Alam Khan argues that the Bahmanis got the weapons from Delhi and that others already had them. Either way, gunpowder weapons became the backbone of the Bahmani army.

After the peaceful reign of Muhammad Shah II (1378-1397), the dynasty fell into turmoil. In 1397 his young son Ghiyasuddin was blinded and imprisoned by the Turkic slave Taghalchin, who put a puppet, Shamsuddin, on the throne. Firuz and Ahmad, grandsons of the founder, marched on Gulbarga, defeated and killed Taghalchin, and in November 1397 Firuz became sultan. He brought Hindus into high office, welcomed Sufis such as Gesudaraz to his court, and was the first author to write in Dakhni, the Deccan form of Urdu. He also founded the city of Firozabad near Gulbarga.

Firuz Shah fought Vijayanagara on many occasions. Early in his reign he turned back Harihara II's advance into the Raichur Doab, and he won victories in 1398 and 1406. The 1406 war ended in a treaty under which Deva Raya I gave his daughter to the sultan in marriage and, according to the Vijayanagara article, agreed to pay a heavy annual tribute of 100,000 huns, pearls and fifty elephants. The Raichur Doab stayed in Bahmani hands for the moment. When Vijayanagara stopped paying, war broke out again, and in 1417 it went against the Bahmanis.

In 1420 Firuz Shah attacked the fort of Pangal, but the campaign ended in disaster. He retreated and gave up the southern and eastern districts of his kingdom, a serious loss of territory, and he was a broken man afterwards. To secure the throne for his son Hasan Khan, he ordered his capable brother Ahmad blinded. Ahmad rebelled and besieged Gulbarga, and in 1422 Firuz abdicated in his favour, dying soon after. He was buried in the Haft Gumbaz tombs at Gulbarga, and his brother began a far more aggressive reign.

Ahmad Shah I, sultan from 1422, spent his reign at war. He fought Vijayanagara in 1423 and campaigned against Warangal in 1424-1425, finally capturing the remnants of the Warangal kingdom in eastern Telangana. He annexed Mahur in the north by 1427, after three campaigns, and fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat from 1425 to 1435. Chroniclers also describe his massacres, including the killing of the Raja of Mahur after his surrender. The conquest of Warangal pushed the Bahmani frontier east across Telangana, into the old heartland of the Kakatiya kings.

Ahmad Shah I moved the Bahmani capital north-east from Gulbarga to Bidar, where he built the great Bidar Fort. The Bahmani Sultanate article dates the move to 1429, the article on Ahmad Shah to 1432, and the Deva Raya II article to around 1426. After settling in Bidar, Ahmad Shah converted to Shi'ism, and he and his successors began to recruit foreigners from overseas into their service. This planted the rivalry between the newcomers, the Afaqis, and the older Deccani nobility, descendants of the first settlers from northern India, that would later tear the sultanate apart.

Ahmad Shah's son Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II, sultan from 1436, faced a revived Vijayanagara under Deva Raya II, who had built up his army with Muslim archers and cavalry. War broke out in 1443. After mixed fortunes, Vijayanagara forces fell back to Mudgal and lost some land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna. In 1445 the sultan was honoured with the Chand Minar, a tall minaret at Daulatabad, for the victory, which was the last major conflict between the two powers. At home, though, rivalry between Deccani and foreign nobles grew, and in 1446 a massacre of Persian Shi'a nobles shook the court.

Mahmud Gawan was a Persian merchant who landed at the port of Dabhol in 1453, aged 42, intending to sell horses to the Bahmani court. Sultan Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II received him well, and Humayun Shah made him chief minister. Under the boy sultans Nizam Shah and Muhammad Shah III he served as regent, and from 1466 he was prime minister and the real ruler of the state. He helped push back a Gajapati invasion from Odisha that came near Bidar, repelled several attacks from Malwa, and in 1469 won the Konkan from Vijayanagara. Under him the sultanate reached its greatest extent.

Gawan, who had first come to the Deccan to sell horses, understood the value of the west coast ports. In February 1472 he captured Goa, long held by Vijayanagara, along with Dabhol, and he took Belgaum using mines and explosives; Bahmani cannon had already been used in the siege of Machal fort in 1470 or 1471. The conquests gave the sultanate a coastline on the Arabian Sea and its widest territory. In the same year Gawan completed his madrasa at Bidar, a great college of religious and secular learning with a library of about 3,000 manuscripts.

To hold such a large state together, Mahmud Gawan reformed its government in 1473. He increased the provinces (tarafs) from four to eight, dividing them equally between Deccani and foreign nobles, limited each provincial governor to a single fort, and standardised the nobles' obligations to the crown. The reforms strengthened the sultan's grip, but many nobles resented losing power. Gawan, a foreign-born Persian, was also caught between the two great factions: the Dakhanis, the Deccan's Sunni elite descended from northern settlers, and the Afaqis, mostly Shi'a newcomers from the west.

Gawan's enemies, angered by reforms that curbed their power, forged a letter that seemed to show him inviting the Gajapati king Purushottama Deva of Odisha to invade. Sultan Muhammad Shah III believed it and on 5 April 1481 had his minister executed, an act he regretted until his own death in 1482. The plot's chief architect, Malik Hasan, also known as Nizam-ul-Mulk Bahri, succeeded Gawan as prime minister and became regent for the next sultan, Mahmud Shah. Without Gawan the sultanate fell into disarray, and power drained from the throne to the provincial governors.

Mahmud Shah, sultan from 1482, was the last Bahmani ruler with real power, and even he depended on his ministers. In 1490 three provincial governors, Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar, Yusuf Adil Shah of Bijapur and Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk of Berar, agreed to assert their independence and founded their own sultanates, though they still professed loyalty to the sultan. Golconda and Bidar soon became independent in practice too. The last Bahmani sultans were puppets of their Barid Shahi ministers, and after 1518 the state broke up into the five Deccan Sultanates; it was formally dissolved in 1527.
